title: Numerical Evaluation of ZX Calculus Optimization for Solovay Kitaev Quantum Circuit Synthesis
authors: Dulari De Silva, Anuradha Mahasinghe, Chon-Fai Kam, Kaushika De Silva, Frederic Cadet, Jingbo Wang
abstract: Fault-tolerant architectures implement non-Clifford T gates through magic-state distillation, so the T-count of a synthesized circuit dominates its physical cost. The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm approximates any single-qubit unitary from a finite gate set with a sequence length that grows only polylogarithmically in the inverse target error, but it optimizes for numerical convergence rather than circuit economy, and its output carries structural redundancy that a gate-level compiler cannot see. We report a measurement of what diagrammatic post-processing recovers from that redundancy. Twelve hundred random single-qubit targets, spanning the three Pauli rotation families and the general gate U(theta, phi, lambda), are synthesized over Clifford+T at three recursion depths, translated into graph-like ZX-diagrams, simplified by automated rewriting, and extracted back to circuits. Post-processing removes 26.6-30.1% of the total gate count and 18.5-22.2% of the T-count. The absolute saving grows with recursion depth, from about 60 to about 1600 gates, while the fractional saving does not: it rises slightly from the shallowest setting and is then flat across a twenty-five-fold change in circuit length, and by the deepest setting the four target families are no longer distinguishable from one another. Because the rewrite rules preserve the implemented linear map, the approximation error is unchanged. The compile-time cost of the rewriting layer, by contrast, grows sharply with depth and comes to dominate the synthesis itself.
summary: This work quantifies the structural redundancy present in quantum circuits generated by the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm. By employing diagrammatic post-processing via ZX-calculus, the authors demonstrate that significant portions of the gate count and T-count can be removed without affecting the implemented quantum operation. This suggests a powerful, systematic optimization pathway for compiling complex quantum circuits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the structural redundancy inherent in quantum circuits synthesized using the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm for approximating arbitrary single-qubit unitaries.
main_result: Diagrammatic post-processing using ZX-calculus rewriting successfully recovers a significant fraction of this redundancy, removing 26.6-30.1% of the total gate count and 18.5-22.2% of the T-count.
method: The authors synthesize target unitaries using Solovay-Kitaev, map the resulting gate sequences to ZX-diagrams, and then apply automated graph-theoretic rewriting rules to simplify the structure.
model_or_system: The model is fault-tolerant quantum computation, specifically synthesizing single-qubit unitaries ($U \in SU(2)$) using the Clifford+T gate set.
key_observables: Total gate count, T-count, and the percentage reduction achieved after post-processing.
important_parameters: Recursion depth (controls approximation level $\epsilon_k$), target unitary family ($R_x, R_y, R_z, U(	heta, \phi, \lambda)$), and the required precision $\epsilon$.
main_assumptions: The comparison is against unoptimized Solovay-Kitaev output, and the compile-time cost of the rewriting layer can become dominant at deep recursion levels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the fundamental rewrite rules of the ZX-calculus and show the evolution of gate/T-count reduction versus recursion depth.
paper_structure: The paper details the synthesis process, the mapping to ZX-diagrams, the application of automated rewriting rules, and quantitative measurements comparing the initial circuit size to the optimized size across various depths and targets.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous analysis of structural redundancy and the development of efficient compilation techniques using diagrammatic methods (ZX-calculus) provides valuable theoretical tools applicable to optimizing quantum simulations in AMO physics.
